tagline: An eighth-century country prophet's indictment of Jerusalem's rulers for injustice, set beside promises of a coming ruler from Bethlehem and a God who delights in mercy.
overview:
Micah came from Moresheth, a small town in the foothills southwest of Jerusalem, and preached during the reigns of Jotham, Ahaz, and Hezekiah, kings of Judah, in the second half of the eighth century BC. He was a contemporary of Isaiah, and he watched the Assyrian empire destroy the northern kingdom of Israel and then invade Judah. His book moves back and forth between judgment and hope. He charges the leaders of Jerusalem and Samaria with seizing land, perverting justice for bribes, and preaching comfort for pay, and he warns that Samaria will become rubble and that even Zion will be plowed like a field.

Yet each section of the book also turns toward hope. God will gather a remnant like a shepherd gathering sheep. In the last days the nations will stream to the mountain of the LORD to learn his ways, and swords will be beaten into plowshares (4:1-3, a passage that also appears in Isaiah 2:2-4). A ruler will come from little Bethlehem whose origins are from of old (5:2). In a courtroom scene God summarizes what he asks of his people: to act justly, to love mercy, and to walk humbly with God (6:8). The book ends with a hymn that plays on Micah's own name, which means who is like the LORD: no God is like the one who pardons iniquity and delights in loving devotion.

Micah matters because it joins two things that are often separated: a fierce concern for how the powerful treat the weak, and a deep hope rooted in God's faithfulness to his promises. Its words were remembered for a century (Jeremiah 26:18 quotes Micah 3:12), and its promise about Bethlehem was cited when wise men came looking for a newborn king (Matthew 2:5-6).
author:
The book is attributed to "Micah the Moreshite" (1:1), a prophet from Moresheth-gath (1:14) in the Shephelah, the lowland hill country between Judah's central mountains and the coastal plain. He is not called the son of anyone, and he is sometimes thought to have been a man of the countryside rather than of Jerusalem's elite, which may explain his anger at landlords who swallowed up small farms. Jeremiah 26:18 confirms that a prophet named Micah of Moresheth preached in Hezekiah's day and quotes his warning about Zion.

Scholars agree that much of chapters 1 to 3 comes from Micah himself. Views differ on the rest. Many critical scholars think chapters 4 to 7, or parts of them, were added by later editors during or after the exile, pointing to passages such as 4:10 (which names Babylon) and 7:8-20 (which seems to presuppose a ruined Jerusalem). Other scholars hold that the whole book, or most of it, goes back to Micah, arguing that eighth-century prophets could and did speak of both judgment and restoration, and that Babylon was already a restless power in Hezekiah's time.
date: Micah 1:1 places his ministry in the reigns of Jotham (about 750 to 735 BC, including a period as co-regent), Ahaz (about 735 to 715 BC), and Hezekiah (about 715 to 686 BC). Micah 1:6 speaks of Samaria's coming destruction, so at least that oracle comes before 722 BC, when Samaria fell to Assyria. Jeremiah 26:18 places his warning about Jerusalem in Hezekiah's reign, and the disaster sweeping toward Jerusalem in 1:10-16 fits the Assyrian invasion of Judah under Sennacherib in 701 BC. A ministry from about 740 to about 700 BC is a common estimate. Those who see later additions date them to the exile or the period after it.
setting:
The Assyrian empire dominated Micah's world. Tiglath-pileser III (about 745 to 727 BC) turned Assyria into an empire that deported conquered peoples. His successors besieged and destroyed Samaria in 722 BC, ending the northern kingdom. In 701 BC Sennacherib invaded Judah, captured many of its fortified towns, and besieged Jerusalem, which was spared (2 Kings 18-19, Isaiah 36-37). Sennacherib's palace at Nineveh was decorated with carved reliefs of his siege of Lachish, one of the towns Micah names (1:13); those reliefs are now in the British Museum. Many of the towns in Micah 1:10-16 lay in the Shephelah near his home, directly in the invader's path.

Inside Judah, the eighth century had brought wealth to some and loss to many. Land was supposed to stay within families as an inheritance from God (Leviticus 25, 1 Kings 21), but powerful men accumulated estates by debt, pressure, and corrupt courts. Isaiah, Micah's contemporary in Jerusalem, condemned the same practice: woe to those who add house to house and field to field (Isaiah 5:8).
purpose: Micah preached to Judah and Jerusalem, and first of all to their rulers, priests, and prophets, calling them to account for injustice and false security. He wanted them to see that the Assyrian threat was God's judgment on their sin, not a random event, and that their confidence that "the LORD is among us" would not protect them while they robbed the poor. At the same time, the book in its final form was preserved for generations who had seen that judgment fall, and it assured them that God would gather a remnant, raise up a faithful ruler, and keep the promises he swore to Abraham and Jacob (7:20). Jeremiah 26:18-19 records that Hezekiah heeded Micah's warning and that the disaster was delayed, which shows how later readers understood the purpose of his preaching: to bring repentance.
story: Micah preached during the years covered by 2 Kings 15-20 and 2 Chronicles 27-32, when Samaria fell and Jerusalem survived Sennacherib's siege. He was a contemporary of Isaiah in Judah and, early on, of Hosea in Israel; Amos had preached a little before him. In the canon Micah stands sixth among the twelve Minor Prophets, after Jonah and before Nahum, a book about the fall of Nineveh. Micah's promises look beyond his own time to the Babylonian exile, the return, and a coming ruler of David's line, and they feed directly into the New Testament's account of Jesus' birth in Bethlehem.
christ:
The best known link is Micah 5:2, which promises a ruler from Bethlehem Ephrathah, small among the clans of Judah, whose origins are from ancient times. When Herod asked where the Messiah was to be born, the chief priests and scribes answered from this verse (Matthew 2:5-6), and John 7:42 shows that people in Jesus' day expected the Messiah to come from Bethlehem. Micah 5:4 adds that this ruler will shepherd his flock in the strength of the LORD, and Jesus called himself the good shepherd (John 10).

Other links are thematic. The vision of nations streaming to Zion to learn God's ways (4:1-3) finds a beginning in the gospel going out from Jerusalem to the nations (Luke 24:47, Acts 1:8). Micah 7:6, about a man's enemies being the members of his own household, is quoted by Jesus in Matthew 10:35-36. And the closing hymn to a God who pardons iniquity and casts sins into the depths of the sea is fulfilled, in Christian reading, in the forgiveness won by Christ.
reading:
Micah is prophetic poetry, compressed and vivid. The book is commonly divided into three cycles, each opening with the command "Hear" (1:2, 3:1, 6:1) and each moving from judgment to hope. Watch for wordplay, especially in 1:10-16, where the names of towns are turned into puns about their fate. Watch for the courtroom scene of chapter 6, where God brings a lawsuit against his people and calls the mountains as witnesses.

Two cautions help. First, Micah's hope passages are not a denial of his warnings; the book holds both, and the reader should not flatten it into only doom or only comfort. Second, Micah 6:8 is often quoted alone as a summary of religion without God's grace. In context it answers a people trying to buy God's favor with offerings, and it comes from a God who has already redeemed them from Egypt (6:4). It is a description of the life of a redeemed people, not a ladder to earn redemption.

structure.title: First cycle: judgment on Samaria and Judah, then a remnant gathered
structure.summary: God comes in judgment on Samaria and Jerusalem; the towns of the Shephelah mourn; land-grabbers are condemned. The cycle ends with the LORD gathering the remnant like sheep.

structure.title: Second cycle: corrupt leaders, then a coming ruler
structure.summary: Rulers, prophets, and priests are indicted and Zion's fall is announced. Then the mountain of the LORD is raised, the scattered are gathered, and a ruler comes from Bethlehem.

structure.title: Third cycle: God's lawsuit, then his unmatched mercy
structure.summary: God brings a case against his people and states what he requires. Micah laments the corruption of society, then waits for God and ends with a hymn to the God who pardons.

themes.title: Justice for the powerless
themes.body: Micah's harshest words are for those with power who use it to take fields, houses, and inheritances from ordinary families (2:1-2), for judges who take bribes, and for leaders who treat the people like meat for the pot (3:1-3). For Micah, injustice is not a side issue to worship; it is the reason worship has become offensive to God.

themes.title: False security
themes.body: Jerusalem's leaders said, "Is not the LORD among us? No disaster can come upon us" (3:11). Micah answers that God's presence is not a guarantee for those who defy him. Temple, priesthood, and prophets bought for pay cannot protect a city built with bloodshed.

themes.title: The remnant and the shepherd
themes.body: Again and again Micah pictures God as a shepherd who gathers the lame, the outcast, and the scattered (2:12, 4:6-7, 7:14), and a coming ruler who shepherds in the LORD's strength (5:4). Judgment is not God's last word; a remnant will be gathered and restored.

themes.title: The nations and Zion
themes.body: Micah sees a day when the nations will come to God's mountain to learn his ways and will abandon war (4:1-4). The same book also speaks of the nations' judgment. God's rule extends to all peoples, both in justice and in blessing.

themes.title: Who is like the LORD?
themes.body: The book closes by playing on Micah's name: no God is like the one who pardons iniquity, does not retain his anger forever, and delights in loving devotion (7:18). The final ground of hope is God's own character and his oath to Abraham and Jacob.

keyChapters.why: Micah's attack on those who seize land and inheritances, and his first promise of a gathered remnant.
The indictment of rulers, priests, and prophets and the warning that Zion will be plowed like a field, remembered a century later in Jeremiah 26:18.
The nations stream to the mountain of the LORD and beat swords into plowshares, the same vision found in Isaiah 2:2-4.
The promise of a ruler from Bethlehem, cited in Matthew 2:6.
God's lawsuit against his people and the summary of what he requires: justice, mercy, and humble walking with God.
The book's closing hymn to the God who pardons and keeps his promises to Abraham and Jacob.

parts.body:
Micah is the sixth of the twelve shorter prophets, seven chapters long. Micah came from Moresheth, a small town in the foothills southwest of Jerusalem, and preached in the reigns of Jotham, Ahaz and Hezekiah, kings of Judah, in the second half of the eighth century BC. He was a contemporary of Isaiah, and he watched Assyria destroy the northern kingdom and then invade Judah.

His book moves back and forth between judgment and hope. He charges the leaders of Jerusalem and Samaria with seizing land, bending justice for bribes, and preaching comfort for pay. He warns that Samaria will become rubble and that even Zion ‘will be plowed like a field’ (3:12).

Yet each part of the book turns toward hope. God will gather a remnant like a shepherd. In the last days the nations will stream to the mountain of the LORD, and swords will be beaten into plowshares (4:1-3). A ruler will come from little Bethlehem (5:2). God sums up what he asks of his people: ‘to act justly, to love mercy, and to walk humbly with your God’ (6:8). The book ends with a hymn that plays on Micah's own name, which means who is like the LORD: ‘Who is a God like You, who pardons iniquity’ (7:18)?

parts.h: Where it sits in the story
parts.body:
Micah belongs to the same years as 2 Kings 15 to 20 and Isaiah 1 to 39. He saw the northern kingdom fall in 722 BC and Sennacherib's army sweep through Judah in 701 BC. He was a countryman, and the towns he names in chapter 1 lay near his home, in the invader's path.

His words were remembered for a century. When Jeremiah was on trial for warning that the temple would fall, elders reminded the crowd that ‘Micah the Moreshite prophesied in the days of Hezekiah’ (Jeremiah 26:18), quoting 3:12, and that Hezekiah had listened and turned to the LORD. One of his great promises also stands in Isaiah almost word for word: the nations streaming to Zion (Micah 4:1-3; Isaiah 2:2-4).

The book is the word of the LORD to ‘Micah the Moreshite’ (1:1), from Moresheth-gath in the Shephelah, the low hill country between Judah's central mountains and the coastal plain. He is not called anyone's son, and he is often thought to have been a man of the countryside rather than of Jerusalem's elite, which may explain his anger at landlords who swallowed up small farms.

Scholars agree that much of chapters 1 to 3 comes from Micah himself. Views differ on the rest. Many critical scholars think chapters 4 to 7, or parts of them, were added by later editors during or after the exile, pointing to 4:10, which names Babylon, and 7:8-20, which seems to assume a ruined Jerusalem. Others hold that most or all of the book goes back to Micah, arguing that eighth-century prophets spoke of both judgment and restoration, and that Babylon was already a restless power in Hezekiah's time.

The heading names Jotham, Ahaz and Hezekiah. The word against Samaria (1:6) must come before 722 BC, and the disaster sweeping toward Jerusalem in 1:10-16 fits Sennacherib's invasion of 701 BC. The book's introduction gives about 740 to about 700 BC as a common estimate; the site's guide to the kings gives 735 to 700.

Assyria dominated Micah's world. Tiglath-pileser III turned it into an empire that deported conquered peoples. His successors besieged and destroyed Samaria in 722 BC. In 701 BC Sennacherib invaded Judah, captured many of its fortified towns and besieged Jerusalem, which was spared. Sennacherib's palace at Nineveh was decorated with carved reliefs of his siege of Lachish, one of the towns Micah names (1:13); those reliefs are now in the British Museum.

Inside Judah, the eighth century had brought wealth to some and loss to many. Land was meant to stay within families as an inheritance from God, but powerful men gathered estates by debt, pressure and corrupt courts. Isaiah, Micah's contemporary in Jerusalem, condemned the same thing: ‘Woe to you who add house to house and join field to field’ (Isaiah 5:8).

The book is commonly divided into three cycles, each opening with the command Hear (1:2; 3:1; 6:1) and each moving from judgment to hope. Chapters 1 and 2 judge Samaria and Jerusalem and end with the remnant gathered like a flock. Chapters 3 to 5 judge the leaders and end with the ruler from Bethlehem. Chapters 6 and 7 bring God's lawsuit and end with the God who pardons.

Micah is prophetic poetry, compressed and vivid. In 1:10-16 he turns the names of towns into puns about their fate. In chapter 6 God takes his people to court and calls the mountains as witnesses.

parts.h: Fields seized, and prophets for hire
parts.body:
‘Woe to those who devise iniquity and plot evil on their beds’ is how chapter 2 opens (2:1). At first light they carry out their plans, because they have the power. ‘They covet fields and seize them; they take away houses’ (2:2). God has a plan of his own: they will lose their land. And the people tell Micah to stop preaching such things. They would rather have a prophet who preaches wine and beer.

Chapter 3 turns on the rulers who should know justice and instead devour the people, a picture of predators feeding on the poor. The prophets announce peace to those who feed them and war to those who do not. Against them Micah says, ‘I am filled with power by the Spirit of the LORD, with justice and courage’ (3:8). Leaders judge for a bribe, priests teach for a price, prophets tell fortunes for money, and all of them say the LORD is among them, so no disaster can come. ‘Therefore, because of you, Zion will be plowed like a field’ (3:12).

Jerusalem was not destroyed in Micah's lifetime. Jeremiah 26 explains why: Hezekiah feared the LORD and sought his favor, and God relented. The warning did its work, and it was fulfilled when Babylon destroyed the city in 587 or 586 BC.

parts.h: Swords into plowshares, and a ruler from Bethlehem
parts.body:
‘In the last days the mountain of the house of the LORD will be established as the chief of the mountains’ (4:1). Many nations will come to learn God's ways. ‘Then they will beat their swords into plowshares and their spears into pruning hooks’ (4:3), and each will sit under his own vine and fig tree, with no one to make him afraid. The same promise stands in Isaiah 2:2-4. Scholars debate whether Micah borrowed from Isaiah, Isaiah from Micah, both from an older oracle known in Jerusalem, or whether later editors added it to both.

War has not ended, and readers ask how this can be. Micah places the vision in the last days. Premillennialists expect a future time when Christ reigns on earth and war ceases. Amillennialists and postmillennialists see it beginning now, as the gospel spreads and peace takes root among Christ's people, and completed in the new creation. Others stress that it calls God's people to live now as citizens of that coming peace. It is not a program any nation can achieve by treaties, and it belongs to no party.

Then comes the promise for which Micah is best known. ‘But you, Bethlehem Ephrathah, who are small among the clans of Judah, out of you will come forth for Me One to be ruler over Israel’ (5:2), one whose origins are from long ago. He will shepherd his flock in the LORD's strength, ‘And He will be our peace’ (5:5). Bethlehem was David's town. God's new ruler will come not from the palace in Jerusalem but from the small place where David's line began.

Chapter 6 is a courtroom. God calls the mountains to hear his case. ‘My people, what have I done to you?’ (6:3). He reminds them that he brought them out of Egypt, redeemed them from slavery, and sent Moses, Aaron and Miriam before them.

A worshiper answers with a question. What should he bring? Burnt offerings, calves, thousands of rams, rivers of oil, even his firstborn? The answer comes: ‘He has shown you, O man, what is good. And what does the LORD require of you but to act justly, to love mercy, and to walk humbly with your God?’ (6:8).

Micah 6:8 is often quoted alone as a summary of religion. In context it answers a people trying to buy God's favor with offerings, and it comes from a God who has already redeemed them (6:4). It describes the life of a redeemed people, not a ladder to earn redemption. It does not abolish worship. It rejects worship used as a bargain. The offer of a firstborn in 6:7 was not idle talk, since kings of Judah had done it and the law forbade it outright. It is named here and not described, and God never asks it.

parts.h: Who is a God like you?
parts.body:
Chapter 7 begins in grief. The faithful have vanished from the land. Officials take bribes, friends cannot be trusted, and families turn on themselves: ‘A man’s enemies are the members of his own household’ (7:6). ‘But as for me, I will look to the LORD; I will wait for the God of my salvation’ (7:7).

The city speaks as one who has fallen but will rise. She will bear God's anger for her sin until he brings her into the light. The prophet prays for God to shepherd his people as in the days of old.

The book closes with a hymn. ‘Who is a God like You, who pardons iniquity and passes over the transgression of the remnant of His inheritance’ (7:18), who does not stay angry forever, because he delights in loving devotion. ‘You will cast out all our sins into the depths of the sea’ (7:19). He will keep faith with Jacob and loving devotion with Abraham, as he swore to their fathers long ago (7:20).

parts.h: How the New Testament reads Micah
parts.body:
When Herod asked where the Messiah was to be born, the chief priests and scribes answered from 5:2: ‘In Bethlehem in Judea,’ they said, and quoted the prophet (Matthew 2:5-6). Matthew's form of the verse speaks of a ruler ‘who will be the shepherd of My people Israel’ (Matthew 2:6). John records that people in Jesus' day expected the Messiah to come from Bethlehem, David's town (John 7:42).

Jesus quoted 7:6 when he warned that following him could divide families: ‘A man’s enemies will be the members of his own household’ (Matthew 10:36).

These are the New Testament's own lines from Micah, and these notes draw no others. Micah's warnings were spoken to Judah by one of its own prophets, and the New Testament never uses them to blame the Jewish people.

Read Micah in its three cycles, and watch each move from judgment to hope. Do not flatten the book into only doom or only comfort. It holds both.

Read the charges for what they name: land seized from families, courts bought, religion for hire. Let them land on yourself before anyone else, and on the powerful of every party. The book's standard is God's covenant, not any modern program.

And read 6:8 where it stands, after God's question, ‘what have I done to you?’, and before the hymn to the God who pardons. Justice, mercy and humility are the shape of a life that has already been rescued.

timeline.what: Jotham reigns in Judah, first as regent for Uzziah. Micah's heading names him (1:1).
Ahaz reigns in Judah and turns to Assyria for help (2 Kings 16).
Micah preaches, by the book's introduction. The site's guide to the kings gives 735 to 700.
Samaria falls to Assyria, as Micah warned (1:6). The guide to the kings, following Thiele, gives 723 or 722.
Hezekiah reigns in Judah and, Jeremiah 26:18-19 says, heeds Micah's warning.
Sennacherib invades Judah, takes Lachish and besieges Jerusalem, which is spared (2 Kings 18 to 19).

timeline.when: Early in Jehoiakim's reign, 609 or after
timeline.what: Elders defend Jeremiah by quoting Micah 3:12 (Jeremiah 26:1, 18).
Babylon destroys Jerusalem, and Zion is plowed like a field (2 Kings 25).

map.title: Judah and Samaria in Micah's day

places.name: Jerusalem
places.line: Zion, whose leaders sold justice (3:9-11). It will be plowed like a field (3:12), and the nations will come to learn there (4:2).

places.name: Samaria
places.line: Israel's capital and hill country, to become a heap of rubble (1:6). Drawn roughly, as a region; the city is not marked.

places.name: Bethlehem
places.line: David's small town, from which God's ruler will come (5:2).

places.name: Gilead
places.line: Rich pasture east of the Jordan, named with Bashan in the prayer for God to shepherd his flock (7:14). Drawn roughly, as a region.

teaching.mapNote: Four places are drawn, each at a point already used on this site's maps; Samaria and Gilead roughly, as regions. Moresheth-gath, Lachish, Gath and the other towns of 1:10-16, and Bashan, are left off, because they are not placed in this site's records. No borders are drawn. The map makes no claim about any border today.
